title: CFR Surveyed 350 Experts About AI’s Future. Here Are the Takeaways. | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: A CFR survey of 350 foreign policy experts on the 2035 AI landscape finds near-unanimity that governance is failing — over 80 percent expect fragmentation, only 5 percent think domestic regulators and courts can keep pace, and over 70 percent think a serious AI accident is the most likely trigger for change. Experts split almost 50/50 on whether frontier capability stays concentrated or diffuses, a divide that maps onto whether scaling laws hold, while roughly 70 percent expect frontier labs to be the most powerful nonstate actors by 2035.

insights.claim: More than 80 percent of 350 surveyed foreign policy experts expect AI governance to be fragmented by 2035, and only 5 percent believe domestic institutions such as regulatory bodies and courts will keep up with the pace of AI development.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: A 5 percent expectation that regulators keep pace means compliance risk to AI business models is expected to arrive late and unevenly rather than as a coordinated regime.
insights.quote: Only 5 percent anticipate that domestic institutions, such as regulatory bodies and courts, will keep up with the pace of AI development.
insights.locator: Experts Agree That Governance Is Failing

insights.claim: Experts see a U.S.-China bilateral agreement as the most likely path to any binding AI governance agreement — a dim prospect given the state of U.S.-China relations, and one that would leave most of the world on the sidelines.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: Global AI rules, if they come, will be set bilaterally by Washington and Beijing — multilateral processes and third-country regimes are not where to look for binding constraints.
insights.quote: A U.S.-China bilateral agreement is the path experts see as the most likely option to produce a binding governance agreement—a dim prospect, given the state of U.S.-China relations
insights.locator: A U.S.-China bilateral agreement is the path

insights.claim: More than 70 percent of respondents say a serious AI accident is the most likely trigger for governance change, implying conditions will get worse before they start to get better.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: Regulation is expected to be crisis-driven, so the risk to AI-exposed assets is a step-function repricing after an incident rather than gradual policy drag.
insights.quote: Taken together, those findings suggest that things will get worse before they start to get better.

themes.theme: The 46/54 split on concentration versus diffusion

insights.claim: Surveyed experts are polarized on how concentrated frontier AI will be in 2035: 46 percent expect the ability to develop frontier capabilities to remain with a few actors while 54 percent predict diffusion to dozens of states and nonstate actors, with few respondents landing between those options.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: A bimodal expert distribution with no middle means the market is pricing an outcome with two very different payoffs for incumbent labs and chip suppliers.
insights.quote: About half (46 percent) expect the ability to develop frontier AI capabilities to remain in the hands of a few actors; 54 percent predict it will diffuse to dozens of states and nonstate actors.
insights.locator: Experts Are Genuinely (and Revealingly) Split on Who Will Build Frontier AI

insights.claim: The concentration-versus-diffusion split maps onto two incompatible technical views: one camp expects scaling laws to hold so that model size, data and compute keep translating into performance and keep frontier development costly and concentrated, while the other expects new models, algorithms, chips or breakthroughs to make frontier AI smaller, cheaper and more widely accessible.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: Whether scaling laws hold is the single variable that determines both market structure and geopolitical distribution of AI power — the key swing factor to monitor.
insights.quote: One group expects scaling laws to hold, and that increases in model size, data, and computing power will reliably translate to improvements in AI performance, keeping frontier AI development costly and, therefore, concentrated.
insights.locator: That polarization likely reflects two incompatible views

insights.claim: Sixty-eight percent of surveyed experts expect productivity gains from AI to concentrate among advanced economies or a small number of private actors rather than spread broadly.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: Consensus expects AI to widen rather than narrow the gap between developed and emerging markets — a structural argument for developed-market equity concentration.
insights.quote: Most experts (68 percent) expect productivity gains from AI to concentrate among advanced economies or a small number of private actors.
insights.locator: The economic stakes of frontier AI development are considerable

insights.claim: Sixty-four percent of respondents say the Global South could only receive meaningful benefits from AI through a fundamental shift away from models that demand enormous data, energy and compute toward less resource-intensive alternatives, meaning new alliances or political strategy alone will not change the calculus.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: Emerging-market AI adoption is gated by the resource intensity of current architectures, so efficiency breakthroughs — not aid or diplomacy — are the unlock to watch.
insights.quote: 64 percent say receiving meaningful benefits from AI would require a fundamental shift in how AI is built—one that moves away from models demanding enormous data, energy, and compute, and toward alternatives that are less resource intensive.
insights.locator: Experts are skeptical that new alliances or political strategy

themes.theme: Power shifting from states to frontier labs

insights.claim: Almost 70 percent of surveyed experts believe frontier AI labs will be the most powerful nonstate actors by 2035, and 75 percent expect nonstate actors generally to gain leverage over the state.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: If labs become the dominant nonstate power center, their equity and governance structures become geopolitical variables, not just corporate ones.
insights.quote: Almost 70 percent of respondents believe frontier AI labs will be the most powerful nonstate actors by 2035, and 75 percent expect nonstate actors to gain leverage over the state.
insights.locator: Power Is Already Shifting From States to Labs

insights.claim: That shift is already visible: at the Group of Seven Summit in June 2026 world leaders were joined by the CEOs of OpenAI, DeepMind, Anthropic, Mistral and other companies to discuss AI governance, AI infrastructure and international stability.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: Lab CEOs now sit at head-of-state forums, which means policy outcomes on compute and infrastructure will be shaped by the firms most exposed to them.
insights.quote: at the Group of Seven Summit in June 2026, world leaders were joined by the CEOs of OpenAI, DeepMind, Anthropic, Mistral, and other companies to discuss AI governance, AI infrastructure, and international stability
insights.locator: Those predictions are already coming true

insights.claim: Alongside labor market disruption and democratic backsliding, respondents named regulatory capture — AI labs gaining power over the governments meant to oversee them — as one of their top concerns.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: Expert consensus expects the AI industry to shape its own rules, which lowers the probability of binding restrictions on incumbents while raising political-backlash risk.
insights.quote: respondents identified regulatory capture as one of their top concerns, fearing AI labs will gain power over the governments that are meant to oversee them
insights.locator: Along with labor market disruption and democratic backsliding

insights.claim: The overall picture is that experts are split over where AI is heading but nearly unanimous that no one is steering, with frontier AI labs holding the most power and expertise while remaining unaccountable to governments or the publics they affect.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: The absence of an accountable steward is the underpriced systemic risk — it means no institution is positioned to absorb or contain an AI-driven shock.
insights.quote: Experts are split over where AI is heading, but nearly unanimous that no one is steering.
